newsitem.title: USA: Panel dismisses two charges against Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: Panel dismisses two charges against Gingrich.

text.p: The House of Representatives ethics committee on Saturday dismissed two charges against House Speaker Newt Gingrich, but said it was working on four others dealing with alleged illegal campaign contributions and gifts.
The charges alleged Gingrich violated federal bribery statutes in his intervention with government agencies on behalf of contributors to GOPAC, the political action committee he formerly headed.
The committee also dismissed a charge of tax and banking law violations against House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt, but chided him on laxity in filing financial statements.

Gingrich was said to have intervened with the Environmental Protection Agency in an asbestos case and with the International Trade Commission on behalf a cement producer seeking favourable treatment in a trade dispute with Mexico.
The charges had been filed last January by House Democratic Whip David Bonior of Michigan and others.

"The committee has dismissed (the complaints) on the grounds that they do not merit further inquiry," committee chairman Nancy Johnson, Republican-Connecticut, and senior Democrat Jim McDermott of Washington said in a letter to the speaker.
But the letter said the committee "is in the process of obtaining additional information" on four other charges filed in the same complaint and had not reached any conclusions.

These complaints alleged that Gingrich had improperly received $250,000 from GOPAC for personal use and $250,000 for campaign purposes. They alleged funnelling of campaign contribitions to Gingrich by GOPAC and conduct unbecoming to a member of the House.

Bonior told a news conference the ethics committee had "opened a whole new area of investigation into GOPAC" and was moving forward on allegations that Gingrich had used the organisation "as his personal, political slush fund."
The committee also called "moot" a seventh complaint which is part of an investigation by special counsel James Cole into possible tax law violations relating to a tax-free foundation.
The committee this week said it had expanded the scope of its investigation, including on whether Gingrich had provided "reliable, accurate and complete information" about a college course he taught.

Responding to the committee's action on Saturday, Gingrich spokesman Tony Blankley said: "I find it remarkable, and slightly pathetic, that the Democrat Party's sole strategy for regaining control of the House has been to attempt to destroy Newt by filing bogus ethics allegations against him."

In a parallel action the ethics committee also dismissed a complaint against Gephardt filed by Republican Jennifer Dunn of Washington, alleging violations of tax and banking laws in connection with a second home owned by Gephardt.
In a letter to the Missouri Democrat, it chided him for delaying and amending income statements.
